headline: A quiet weekend in the stack, with no new preprint announcements since Friday: the sharpest result still standing is the Intern-NCP team's 8.9-billion-parameter latent-space model, which reaches OLMo-3-7B's final pretraining loss after 51.3 percent of the tokens.

items.title: A graded barrier keeps holes off the oxide, and the dot stays put
items.dek: A 13-author group swapped the flat silicon-germanium barrier above a germanium quantum well — the buried layer that hosts hole spin qubits — for one whose silicon fraction is ramped from 20 to 80 percent, and the gate-voltage window over which a single dot stays stable grew 2.75-fold.
items.why_it_matters: The limit on these devices is not the qubit but the oxide interface a few tens of nanometres above it: holes that collect there become the fluctuating charges that shift the dot's energy levels. Moving the valence-band edge so those states can no longer fill removes the noise source instead of filtering it, which is why the stable gate range widens rather than the noise merely averaging lower.
items.background_md: Hole spin qubits in germanium are built by burying a thin strained-germanium layer under a silicon-germanium barrier and using surface gates to squeeze out single holes. Everything about the device is set by how quiet the electrostatic environment is: one charge trapped at the barrier-to-dielectric interface a few tens of nanometres away shifts the dot's energy levels, and that charge noise is what limits how long a spin holds its phase. The barrier is therefore asked to do two incompatible things at once — hold the carriers away from the dirty interface, and still let the gates reach through it.
items.deeper_md:
The reference stack is 400 nm of Si₀.₂Ge₀.₈, a 15 nm germanium well, then a 35 nm Si₀.₂Ge₀.₈ top barrier. The modified stack keeps only 10 nm of Si₀.₂Ge₀.₈ as a spacer and replaces the remaining 25 nm with SiₓGe₁₋ₓ graded from x = 0.2 to x = 0.8. More silicon lowers the valence-band maximum, so at the gate voltages that populate the dot there is no longer a hole state available at the SiGe-to-dielectric interface for a carrier to sit in.

Measured consequences: a 2.75-fold expansion of the stable gate range, no observable voltage drift over hours in the few-hole regime, and charge noise down to 0.46 µeV/√Hz at 1 Hz, rising to 6.77 µeV/√Hz at 10 mHz and 46.48 µeV/√Hz at 1 mHz. Magnetotransport showed comparable saturation mobility and the same integer quantum Hall features as the reference, so stability was not bought by degrading transport.

The caveat is that the 1 Hz figure is not a record — Lodari and co-workers reported charge noise below a 0.2 µeV/√Hz detection floor in 2020, with a channel 55 nm below the interface — so the claim worth checking is the width of the stable gate window, not the headline noise number.

glossary.definition: The square root of the power spectral density of random shifts in a quantum dot's energy level, quoted at a stated frequency; it sets how fast a spin qubit loses phase coherence.
The top of the energy band that holes occupy; moving it up or down by changing alloy composition decides where in a layer stack holes will accumulate.
A silicon-germanium alloy that is 20 percent silicon; both its lattice constant and its band edges shift with the silicon fraction, which is why composition is usable as a design knob.
The operating point at which a quantum dot holds only a handful of holes, where the remaining energy levels are far enough apart that a single spin can be addressed.

items.fab_angle: The whole result is a deposition-control problem: the graded 25 nm section needs the silicon fraction walked from 0.2 to 0.8 inside one epitaxy run, as a gas-ratio ramp with no metrology step available in between.

sources.title: Enhancing charge stability of Ge quantum well heterostructures via SiGe layer composition engineering
Impact of interface traps on charge noise, mobility and percolation density in Ge/SiGe heterostructures

items.title: Calibrating a terahertz receiver against caesium, not another meter
items.dek: A four-author group used caesium atoms promoted to a high-lying Rydberg state to measure the electric field coming out of a commercial 204 GHz photomixer transmitter directly in volts per metre, with no calibrated reference detector anywhere in the measurement chain.
items.why_it_matters: Every conventional field measurement above 100 GHz is a comparison against another instrument whose own calibration traces back through a chain of transfer standards, and uncertainty accumulates at every link in that chain. An atomic measurement replaces the chain with a dipole matrix element and a pair of fundamental constants, which is what lets a photomixer receiver's own noise floor be quoted as an absolute field — 1.7 mV/m — rather than as a current in picoamps that means nothing without a separate calibration.
items.background_md: Above roughly 100 GHz there is no practical absolute standard for electric field strength. Power meters, horns and detectors are calibrated against one another, and the reference chain grows longer and less certain the higher in frequency you go. Rydberg atoms offer a different route: promote an outer electron to a state with a large principal quantum number and the atom acquires an enormous transition dipole moment, so even a weak field at the right frequency splits its optical absorption line by an amount fixed only by the field itself and by constants that are already known to high accuracy.
items.deeper_md:
The measured transition is caesium 17D₅/₂ → 18P₃/₂, located at 204.518(2) GHz. A field driving that transition splits the probe line by the Rabi frequency Ω = dE/ħ, so mapping the Autler-Townes splitting against detuning recovers Ω, and the averaged dipole matrix element d̄ = 139 ea₀ converts it into a field in volts per metre.

Two transmitter bias points gave 6.5(1) V/m and 13.4(2) V/m after correcting for the vapour cell's two-window transmission, η = 0.77(2); transmitter output across the tested bias range was 1.1(2) to 12(2) µW. Turning those atom-calibrated fields on a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver pins its responsivity at 34(2) nA per V/m, and its 48 pA current-noise floor then becomes 1.7 mV/m, about 0.9 mV/m/√Hz — within roughly 1.5× of the 0.6 mV/m/√Hz Johnson limit the authors compute for it.

The honest caveat is in their own comparison: Rydberg receivers in the millimetre-wave band already reach below 10 µV/m/√Hz, so here the atoms are far better as a ruler than as a detector. And the traceability rests on a calculated dipole moment, not on an independently measured one.

glossary.definition: An atomic state with the outer electron promoted to a high principal quantum number, where the orbit is large enough that the atom couples strongly to microwave and terahertz fields.
The splitting of an optical absorption line into two peaks when a second field drives a coupled transition; the peak separation equals the Rabi frequency, so reading it measures the driving field.
The rate at which a driven two-level system cycles between its states, equal to dE/ħ; it is the bridge from a field in volts per metre to a frequency you can measure on a spectrum.
Electron charge times the Bohr radius, the natural unit for an atomic transition dipole moment; the larger the dipole moment, the weaker the field the atom can resolve.

sources.title: SI-Traceable Calibration and Performance Benchmarking of a Terahertz Photomixer Transmitter-Receiver System Using a Rydberg Atomic Sensor
A self-calibrating SI-traceable broadband Rydberg atom-based radio-frequency electric field probe and measurement instrument
Microwave electrometry via electromagnetically induced absorption in cold Rydberg atoms

items.title: An analog crossbar that reads its answer as a delay, not a current
items.dek: A six-author group replaced the current-sensing readout at the foot of a memristive crossbar — the analog array that multiplies a vector by a matrix in a single step — with a circuit that converts the column voltage into a time delay, shrinking one column's readout from 11,000 to 480 square micrometres.
items.why_it_matters: Analog in-memory computing wins on the multiply and then gives the win back at the edge of the array, where every column needs its own converter and that converter is what the area budget actually goes on. Trading current sensing for a voltage-to-time conversion moves the cost out of area and into conversion latency — here a 2.5 microsecond spike window — which is a trade a spiking network can absorb and a clocked datapath cannot.
items.background_md: A memristive crossbar performs a vector-matrix product in the analog domain: drive the rows with voltages, let each cell's programmed conductance set a current, and let Kirchhoff's current law sum them down the column wire. The multiply itself is close to free. Reading the column out is not, because the answer is an analog quantity that has to become a number, and the converter that does it has to be built once per column. In published crossbar accelerators that peripheral circuitry, rather than the array, is what dominates both area and energy.
items.deeper_md:
The proposed readout senses the column voltage and converts it to a pulse delay instead of summing and scaling currents. In 130 nm CMOS, post-layout, the voltage-to-time block measures 480 µm² against 11,000 µm² for the current-sensing baseline — roughly 20× — and costs 0.58 pJ per operation, against a baseline drawing 48 µW, or 120 pJ across the same 2.5 µs window.

The numbers that decide how to read this are the other ones in the paper. Total energy per synaptic operation is 129 pJ, of which the synaptic circuit itself is 128.5 pJ. The readout change is therefore nearly all of the area saving and nearly none of the energy — the opposite of how a 20× result usually gets summarised.

Devices were modelled over 0.1–1 mS for the 10×1 prototype and 1–10 kΩ for a 64×10 digit classifier, with maximum input rate 200 kHz set by the 2.5 µs spike. Two caveats: this is post-layout simulation, not measured silicon, and the digit network is reported as matching the software classification on representative samples rather than as an accuracy figure over a test set.

glossary.definition: A grid of programmable resistors at every row-column crossing; driving the rows with voltages makes each device pass a current set by its conductance, and the column wire adds those currents.
Picojoules spent on one multiply-accumulate; it is the figure that decides whether an analog array is worth the converters bolted to its edge.
A unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance, so 1 mS is 1 kΩ; the conductance range a device can be programmed across sets how many distinct weight levels it can hold.
A simulation run against the parasitic resistance and capacitance extracted from the drawn layout rather than from the schematic — closer to silicon than a schematic run, still not silicon.

items.fab_angle: A voltage-to-time converter is mostly inverters — the paper sizes its block at about 63.5 inverter equivalents — which makes it one of the few analog functions a student cell library at a mature node can realistically lay out and characterise.

items.title: Eight chiplets are enough to build a bespoke accelerator from
items.dek: Fengshui, a design framework from an eight-author group, searches for the smallest pool of chiplets that can be recombined into per-application accelerators, and reports that eight of them land within 4.1 percent of what a design free to invent any chiplet it likes achieves.
items.why_it_matters: The standing objection to building one accelerator per operator is that each one would need its own mask set and its own verification effort. If a fixed pool of eight chiplets covers the space to within a few percent, the number of mask sets stops scaling with the number of applications and starts scaling with the number of distinct dataflows — a far smaller number, and one that moves slowly. What the framework is really claiming is that accelerator diversity is shallower than the design space makes it look.
items.background_md: Deep-learning operators want different hardware from one another. A convolution rewards holding weights still while activations stream past; a large matrix multiply rewards holding partial sums still; an embedding lookup wants the arithmetic sitting next to the memory because there is almost no data reuse to exploit. One homogeneous array has to be a compromise across all of them. Building a separate die per operator is the obvious fix and the impossible one, because each new die carries a fixed mask and verification cost regardless of how many parts eventually ship. Chiplets exist to spread that fixed cost across more than one product.
items.deeper_md:
The framework co-optimises two decisions that normally have to be made in the wrong order: which chiplets exist, and which accelerators get assembled from them. Pools are grown one member at a time — the second addition is a processing-in-memory unit, the third and fourth an expert-parallelism switch and another dataflow, and by five all of row-, output- and weight-stationary plus PIM and switch are represented. The eight-member pool ends up holding three output-stationary, Gemmini-style chiplets that differ only in processing-element count.

Against homogeneous accelerators the generated designs cut energy 48.5% and energy-delay product 93.0%. For datacentre mixture-of-experts and dense-LLM prefill the energy saving is up to 16.8%; for edge autonomous-driving perception it is 12.0% under a real-time latency bound.

Two things to hold onto. The physical claim rests on place-and-route validation at an assumed 14 nm, with the PIM chiplet pinned to a 1Y-nm process taken from a published specification, so the area and cost figures inherit whatever those models get wrong. And the search explicitly excludes algorithm-level rewrites such as FlashAttention-style fusion, which is where a good deal of achievable energy currently comes from.

glossary.definition: Which operand a systolic array refuses to move: keeping partial sums, weights or input rows resident decides what has to be re-read from memory, and therefore where the energy goes.
The one-off cost of getting a design to silicon — masks, verification, physical implementation — paid per design rather than per part, which is why bespoke dies stay rare.
Arithmetic placed inside or beside the memory banks so an operation with almost no data reuse, such as an embedding gather, never has to cross the memory bus.
Energy multiplied by run time; it stops a design claiming an energy win that it obtained purely by running more slowly.

items.fab_angle: Reusing a chiplet means freezing its die-to-die interface before the accelerators that will consume it exist, so a pool like this has to be designed against a published contract — UCIe 3.0's 48 and 64 GT/s rates, and its bump-pitch range from 25 µm down towards 1 µm for 3D stacking.

sources.title: Fengshui: Demystifying Chiplet Ecosystem and Bespoke Neural Network Accelerator Codesign

items.title: Quarantine the name, not the memory
items.dek: A three-author Cambridge group proposes Reinc, a change to CHERI's hardware pointers that stops a freed allocation from sitting unusable while stale pointers to it are tracked down: the slot is handed a fresh identity instead, and on SQLite the number of full memory sweeps falls from 267 to one.
items.why_it_matters: Every capability-based use-after-free defence so far has had the same shape — stop the program, scan memory for pointers that name a dead object, then release it — and the scan is what made the approach unaffordable under allocation-heavy workloads. Recycling the identifier rather than the address decouples how often you sweep from how often the program frees, so the cost of the defence stops tracking allocation rate and starts tracking something the allocator controls.
items.background_md: A use-after-free bug is a pointer that outlives the object it points at. CHERI attacks that by making pointers unforgeable hardware objects — capabilities — carrying their own bounds, permissions and a validity tag, so an out-of-bounds dereference faults rather than silently reading a neighbour. Spatial safety comes almost free that way. Temporal safety does not, because nothing in the pointer records when the object died. The usual remedy tags each allocation with a generation number and quarantines the memory until every capability bearing the old number has been found and revoked, which means periodically sweeping the entire address space.
items.deeper_md:
CHERI-D stores an 8-bit generation ID inline with the allocation, giving 255 lifetimes per slot before the ID is exhausted and the slot must be quarantined. Reinc quarantines the exhausted ID instead: the slot receives a new, unused ID and the memory goes straight back into circulation, while old IDs are reclaimed in the background. Sweep frequency now follows ID exhaustion rather than allocation churn.

On SQLite's speedtest1, Cornucopia Reloaded needed 267 memory sweeps where Reinc needs one — or none with ID-sweep reclamation enabled — and quarantine events fall from about 221,000 to 90. Reported overheads are 1.7% average on SPEC CPU2006 integer, 0.7% on SQLite and 0.3% on PARSEC, at an FPGA cost of 5.27% more LUT logic, 9.02% more registers and 8.98% more LUT memory on the CHERI-Toooba softcore.

Caveats stated plainly: this is posted as a draft, the evaluation runs on an FPGA softcore rather than a fabricated core, and the competing PICASSO design reports about 5% geometric-mean SPEC overhead using a centralised colour table — so the two are trading decentralised metadata locality against table size, not one strictly beating the other.

glossary.definition: A pointer the hardware will not let software forge: it carries bounds, permissions and a validity tag alongside the address, so a dereference outside the named object faults.
Reading or writing through a pointer whose object has already been released; because the allocator may have handed the space to something else, the pointer now addresses another object's data.
Holding freed memory out of service until nothing live can still name it — safe, and the reason temporal-safety schemes run short of address space under allocation-heavy workloads.
The configurable logic element inside an FPGA; quoting a hardware change's cost in LUTs and registers is how it is measured before anyone commits it to a chip.

sources.title: CHERI-D Reincarnate: efficient multicore CHERI temporal memory safety through allocation reincarnation (draft version)
CHERI-D: Secure and efficient inline object ID for CHERI temporal memory safety
PICASSO: Scaling CHERI Use-After-Free Protection to Millions of Allocations using Colored Capabilities

items.title: Reorder the tiles so the network gets a drip, not a flood
items.dek: Entwine, from a five-author group, changes the order in which a GPU works through the tiles of a matrix multiply so that finished results appear at a steady rate for the network to send, and reports a 1.232× geometric-mean speedup over running cuBLAS and NCCL one after the other.
items.why_it_matters: Overlapping communication with computation is usually treated as a scheduling problem sitting outside the kernel. Making the kernel's own output rate the quantity being tuned, and then paying for the transfers out of an explicitly measured share of the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, turns overlap into a resource-allocation problem with a number on both sides — which is the form in which it can be optimised rather than guessed at.
items.background_md: Splitting a model across several GPUs means every layer ends in a collective — an all-reduce or a reduce-scatter — in which each device contributes its partial result and each ends up with the combination. The arithmetic is done in tiles, and a tile finishes long before the whole tensor does, so in principle the network can start moving the first tile while the last is still being computed. In practice the two compete for the same silicon: on NVIDIA hardware the collective library implements each operation as its own kernel, so bytes on the wire and floating-point work are contending for the same streaming multiprocessors.
items.deeper_md:
Three coupled decisions. First, tile order: a conventional traversal finishes tiles in bursts, which starves the link and then floods it, so Entwine reorders the traversal to make the production rate roughly constant. Second, the communication path: rather than handing finished tiles to a separate collective kernel, it issues fine-grained transfers from the streaming multiprocessors themselves, which is what keeps per-tile latency low enough for the smoothed schedule to be worth anything. Third, the split: because the communication work consumes SM slots, the allocation between compute and communication is optimised rather than left to the runtime.

Across tensor-parallel LLM workloads the reported gain is 1.232× geometric mean and 1.433× maximum against cuBLAS plus NCCL, and 3.1–9.8% geometric mean against existing overlap schemes. The second figure is the one to read: beating a non-overlapped baseline by 23% is table stakes for this class of work.

Caveats: the implementation is not public yet — the authors promise it on publication — and the evaluation is confined to tensor-parallel LLM workloads, so nothing here says what happens to a schedule whose communication is not a per-layer collective.

glossary.definition: A sub-block of a matrix multiply sized so its operands fit in on-chip memory; the full product is computed as a sequence of tiles, which is why partial results become available early.
The GPU's independently scheduled compute unit; kernels are allocated SMs, so a communication kernel and a compute kernel running at once are dividing a fixed pool between them.
A collective in which every device contributes a partial result and every device ends up holding the combined one; it is how tensor-parallel layers reconcile their pieces, and it is synchronous.
NVIDIA's dense linear-algebra library and its collective-communication library; together they are the default implementation any overlap scheme has to beat to be interesting.

items.title: A model that predicts the next idea as well as the next token
items.dek: The Intern-NCP team trained an 8.9-billion-parameter model with a second objective running alongside next-token prediction: predict the next multi-token concept, drawn from a vocabulary the model builds by quantising its own hidden states, and reach a 7-billion baseline's final pretraining loss on 51.3 percent of the tokens.
items.why_it_matters: Every training token is bought, so an objective that reaches the same loss on roughly half of them is a claim about data efficiency rather than about benchmark position. The mechanism is what makes the claim checkable: the concept vocabulary comes out of the model's own activations rather than from a separate sentence encoder, so there is no external embedding space whose quality could be quietly doing the work.
items.background_md: A language model is trained to predict one token at a time, which means most of the loss signal comes from choices that are locally almost forced — the second half of a word, the closing bracket. Several lines of work have tried adding an objective at a coarser scale, so that part of the gradient carries information about what the next sentence or the next step of an argument will be. The hard part is defining the coarse unit: it has to be discrete enough to predict and rich enough to be worth predicting, and whichever encoder supplies it becomes a second system whose failures are hard to separate from the model's own.
items.deeper_md:
The concept vocabulary is built by product-quantising the model's own hidden states, so the discrete units originate inside the network — the difference from Meta's Large Concept Models, which predicted inside the fixed SONAR sentence-embedding space. A dedicated Concept Module predicts the next concept and feeds the prediction back down to condition ordinary token-level generation, with both objectives trained jointly end to end.

Scale is 8.9B parameters on 5.73T tokens of Dolma-3. Reported results: OLMo-3-7B's final pretraining loss is reached after 51.3% of the total tokens; the finished model is 2.45 points ahead of OLMo-3-7B on a downstream macro-average, with a 5.99-point gain on GSM8K; and against a parameter-matched 8.9B baseline it approaches the same loss using 85% of the computation. The 17M-parameter quantisation module can be retrained on its own for domain adaptation, and injecting concept representations into a speculative-decoding drafter lifts mean accepted length by 4.17%.

All of it is self-reported with no third-party replication, and the headline comparison is against a 7B model from another lab. The parameter-matched comparison is the one that carries the weight, and it is the smaller number.

glossary.definition: Splitting a vector into sub-vectors and replacing each with the nearest entry in its own small codebook, so a few modest codebooks between them index an enormous number of distinct vectors.
The average negative log-probability a model assigns to the next token on held-out text; it is the quantity scaling laws predict, which is why matching it on fewer tokens is the claim being made.
The unweighted mean of scores across a set of benchmarks, so a small benchmark counts as much as a large one and no single task can carry the headline number.
In speculative decoding, the average number of tokens a small drafter proposes before the large model rejects one; it sets the achievable speedup directly.

foundations.subtitle: Sub-nanometre motion with no bearings, and the hysteresis, creep and drift you have to design around.
foundations.tldr: A piezoelectric stack turns volts straight into strain, so its resolution is limited by how quietly you can hold a voltage rather than by any mechanical step size: on one vendor's actuator, 0.3 mV of drive noise is 0.2 nm of motion. The stack is guided by a flexure, a mechanism that moves by bending rather than sliding, so there is no friction to stick and no clearance to take up. What you pay for that is a device that does not go where you told it — the same voltage gives a different position depending on which direction you came from, and it keeps creeping for hours after you stop.

sections.heading: Why a screw cannot get you to a nanometre
sections.body_md:
Start with the thing being replaced. A leadscrew stage turns rotation into translation through a threaded nut, and every part of that chain stops being a machine at some scale and becomes a pile of contacting surfaces. The nut and screw have clearance, so reversing direction moves the motor before it moves the stage — backlash. The sliding or rolling elements have a static friction larger than their kinetic friction, so a small commanded move builds elastic force until the joint breaks free and overshoots — stick-slip. Neither is a manufacturing defect you can polish out; both follow from having two solid bodies in contact that have to slide past each other.

A piezoelectric actuator sidesteps the whole category. The material itself changes length when you apply a field, so there is no joint, no clearance and nothing to break free. The commanded quantity is a voltage, and the smallest move you can make is set by the smallest voltage change you can hold steady.

sections.heading: What the ceramic actually does
sections.body_md:
The workhorse material is lead zirconate titanate, PZT. As fired it is useless: the crystal domains point in random directions and their contributions cancel. It is made piezoelectric by poling — holding it near its Curie temperature in a strong electric field until the domains line up, then cooling with the field still applied, which leaves a permanent net polarisation behind.

After that, a field along the poling direction stretches the ceramic along that direction. The constant that says by how much is d₃₃, the piezoelectric charge constant, defined either as induced charge per unit applied force or, equivalently, as induced strain per unit applied field, and quoted in coulombs per newton. There is a companion constant d₃₁ for the strain produced at right angles to the field, and it carries the opposite sign — stretch along the axis and the ceramic thins across it. Practical actuators are stacks of thin layers wired electrically in parallel and mechanically in series, because strain follows field rather than voltage: thin layers put a useful field across the ceramic at a supply voltage you can actually build.

sections.heading: Flexures: bearings that work by bending
sections.body_md:
A piezo stack pushes hard along one axis and resists everything else poorly, so it has to be guided. The guide is a flexure: a single piece of metal with thin necks machined into it, arranged so the mechanism deforms elastically along the intended axis and is stiff in every other direction. There are no sliding surfaces anywhere, which is the entire point. No sliding means no friction and therefore no stick-slip; no clearance means no backlash; no wear means the mechanism behaves the same after a million cycles as after ten; and no lubricant means it works in vacuum and in the cold. A precision cryogenic stage built for an astronomical spectrograph drives its detector with piezo actuators on a flexure guide for exactly that reason — it has to operate at 120 K, where any grease stopped being a liquid long ago.

Flexures charge for this. The mechanism is a spring, so the actuator spends part of its force stretching the guide rather than moving the load, and the assembly has a mechanical resonance that caps how fast it can be driven.

sections.heading: The three lies: hysteresis, creep, drift
sections.body_md:
The bad news comes from the same domain physics that made the material work. The domains do not follow the field reversibly; they switch with a lag, so the length you get at a given voltage depends on whether you arrived from above or below. Plot displacement against voltage over a full cycle and you get an open loop rather than a line. That is hysteresis, and because the shape of the loop depends on how fast you traverse it, compensating for it needs a rate-dependent model — in a long-stroke piezo-stepper assembling 500 µm of travel out of steps of up to 3 µm, it shows up as velocity ripple within each step across drive frequencies from 0.4 to 100 Hz.

Second, the domains keep reorganising after the voltage stops changing, so the position drifts on in the direction of the last move, decaying roughly logarithmically in time. Third, PZT's coefficients depend on temperature, so a thermally noisy stage is a different instrument from a quiet one. The practical cost: an actuator driven by a straightforward PID controller has been measured tracking a 1 Hz reference with about 2% of its travel range as error, rising to 5.2% at 2 Hz.

sections.heading: Closing the loop, and what it does not fix
sections.body_md:
The remedy is to stop trusting the voltage and measure the position instead. The usual choices are a strain gauge bonded to the stack, an inductive LVDT, or a capacitive sensor reading the gap between plates mounted on the moving and fixed halves of the flexure; capacitive and LVDT are what get used when accuracy or dynamics matter most.

The improvement is large. The same actuator that a PID drove to 2% error at 1 Hz holds roughly 0.9 µm — about 1.2% — under a sliding-mode controller with perturbation estimation, and a commercial closed-loop stage with a capacitive sensor is specified at 0.0447% nonlinearity over a 400 µm stroke, which is 179 nm.

Notice what the loop does not fix. It cannot make the mechanism faster than its first mechanical resonance, because feedback pushed past a lightly damped resonance turns the stage into an oscillator. And it cannot remove noise the sensor itself contributes, because the loop now believes the sensor: sensor noise is injected straight into the stage position.

sections.heading: Where the resolution actually comes from
sections.body_md:
It is worth doing the arithmetic that fixes the resolution, because it explains why these systems are specified the way they are. Take an actuator with 100 µm of travel at 150 V. That is about 0.67 µm per volt. Now ask how quietly the amplifier holds its output: at 0.3 mV of noise the stage moves 0.2 nm — and that is precisely the resolution figure published for that combination.

Nothing about the ceramic, the flexure or the control law appears anywhere in that calculation. The resolution of an open-loop piezo stage is a property of its power supply. This is also why the datasheets hedge their resolution numbers with conditions about grounding, shielded cabling, vibration isolation and temperature stability — those are not boilerplate, they are the terms under which the drive-noise figure holds. And it is why a longer-travel actuator has coarser resolution on the same electronics: more micrometres per volt is more nanometres per millivolt of noise.

glossary.definition: The piezoelectric charge constant along the poling axis: induced charge per unit force applied along that axis, or equivalently induced strain per unit field applied along it, in coulombs per newton.

Holding a piezoelectric ceramic near its Curie temperature in a strong electric field so its domains align, then cooling with the field still on. Without it the domains cancel and the part does nothing.
The lost motion when a threaded or geared drive reverses, caused by clearance between the mating parts; it is why a screw stage does not return to the same place from both directions.
The jump that occurs when static friction exceeds kinetic friction: the drive loads the joint elastically until it breaks free, and the joint then overshoots the commanded position.
A mechanism that moves by elastically bending thin sections of one piece of material rather than by sliding, trading limited stroke for the absence of friction, backlash, wear and lubricant.
The continued drift of a piezo actuator's position after the drive voltage has stopped changing, decaying roughly logarithmically in time as the domains keep reorganising.
A linear variable differential transformer — a position sensor that reads a magnetic core's displacement inside a set of coils from the imbalance it creates in their induced voltages.

foundations.try_this: Take whichever instrument in the lab has a micrometre or leadscrew stage — the probe station or a microscope will do — and measure its backlash directly. Pick a feature, drive 50 µm away and back, and read how far the return lands from where it started. Then repeat while always approaching from the same side: the error mostly disappears, and that difference is the entire argument for a flexure. Follow it by reading the hysteresis-modelling section of Ding and Li's 2018 Micromachines paper, which is open access, for the loop a piezo substitutes in its place.
